RIVERBEND REGIONAL TRANSIT AUTHORITY

FISCAL YEAR 2026 ANNUAL PERFORMANCE REPORT
(July 1, 2025 - June 30, 2026)

Accepted by the Board of Directors on September 24, 2026
Prepared by the Office of Planning and Performance

-------------------------------------------------------------------------

MESSAGE FROM THE CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER

Fiscal Year 2026 was the year Riverbend Regional Transit finally moved
past the pandemic. For the first time since 2019, total ridership
exceeded pre-pandemic levels, reaching 9.84 million unlinked passenger
trips, 4.1 percent above FY2019 and 13.6 percent above FY2025. This
growth did not happen by accident. It is the result of the Frequent
Network redesign launched on August 17, 2025, which concentrated service
on fewer, more direct corridors with buses every 15 minutes or better
from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., seven days a week.

We also faced real challenges: an operator shortage that forced us to
cancel more trips than we would like during the fall, rising fuel and
parts costs, and the expiration of federal relief funds that had
supported our operating budget for four years. This report describes
both our progress and the work still ahead, with the same honesty our
riders expect from us.

Lucinda Graves-Mbeki
Chief Executive Officer

-------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. SYSTEM OVERVIEW

Riverbend Regional Transit Authority (RRTA) provides fixed-route bus,
paratransit and microtransit service to the City of Riverbend and eight
surrounding municipalities in Calloway and Dunmore counties, a service
area of 412 square miles with a population of approximately 486,000.
At the end of FY2026, RRTA operated:

- 31 fixed routes, including 9 Frequent Network corridors and 2 bus
  rapid transit lines (the Red Line and the new Blue Line);
- 168 buses in the active fleet, of which 42 are battery-electric;
- the RiverRide paratransit service, with 64 vehicles;
- RRTA Flex on-demand microtransit in four zones.

The agency employs 1,027 people, including 612 bus operators.

2. RIDERSHIP

Fixed-route ridership grew to 9.21 million trips, up 12.3 percent from
FY2025. The nine Frequent Network corridors carried 68 percent of all
fixed-route trips, compared with 55 percent on the same streets before
the redesign. Weekend ridership grew fastest, up 21 percent, reflecting
the decision to run Sunday service at the same frequency as Saturdays.

The Blue Line bus rapid transit, which opened on March 9, 2026 along
Harmon Avenue and Old Mill Road, averaged 7,450 weekday boardings in its
first three full months, well ahead of the forecast of 5,800 used in
its federal grant application.

Paratransit ridership reached 318,000 trips (up 6 percent), and RRTA
Flex carried 311,000 trips, nearly double the previous year, after the
Eastgate and Pine Hollow zones were added in January.

Table 1. Ridership by mode (unlinked trips)
Mode                      FY2025        FY2026      Change
Fixed route (incl. BRT)   8,201,000     9,210,000   +12.3%
Paratransit (RiverRide)     300,000       318,000    +6.0%
Microtransit (Flex)         158,000       311,000   +96.8%
Total                     8,659,000     9,839,000   +13.6%

3. SERVICE RELIABILITY

On-time performance, defined as departing a timepoint no more than one
minute early or five minutes late, averaged 82.7 percent, short of our
target of 85 percent. Performance was strongest on the Red and Blue
Lines (91 and 89 percent), where buses benefit from dedicated lanes and
transit signal priority, and weakest on Routes 4, 12 and 27, which share
congested downtown streets with construction detours.

Missed trips, caused mostly by operator shortages, peaked at 3.8 percent
of scheduled trips in October 2025. After the hiring and retention
measures described in Section 6, the rate fell to 0.9 percent in June
2026. Mean distance between mechanical failures improved from 9,100 to
10,400 miles, thanks largely to the retirement of 23 diesel buses from
2009.

4. SAFETY AND SECURITY

There were 2.1 preventable collisions per 100,000 miles, an improvement
from 2.6 in FY2025. Reported assaults on operators fell from 19 to 11
after the installation of protective operator barriers on the entire
fleet was completed in December. Customer injuries remained low, at 0.4
per 100,000 boardings.

RRTA launched a Transit Ambassador program in partnership with the
Calloway County Department of Behavioral Health, placing 14 trained
ambassadors at the Central Station and on the busiest routes to assist
riders and connect people in crisis with services.

5. CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE

The annual customer satisfaction survey, conducted in April 2026 with
3,212 riders, found that 78 percent were satisfied or very satisfied with
RRTA overall, up from 71 percent. Frequency and the new real-time
arrival screens were the most frequently cited improvements; cleanliness
of shelters and reliability on crosstown routes were the top complaints.

Fare capping was introduced with the Tap&Ride card on November 1, 2025:
riders never pay more than $2.50 per day or $50 per month, regardless of
how many trips they take. By June 2026, 61 percent of fare payments were
made with the card or the mobile app, and 18,400 riders reached the
monthly cap at least once.

6. WORKFORCE

The operator shortage was the most serious operational challenge of the
year. At the start of FY2026, RRTA had 548 operators against a
requirement of 610. The agency responded with:

- a new collective bargaining agreement with Transit Workers Union
  Local 1789, ratified on December 3, 2025, raising the starting
  operator wage from $19.40 to $23.10 per hour;
- paid training with a $3,000 retention bonus after one year;
- an in-house commercial driver's license school that graduated eight
  classes of new operators.

By June 30, 2026, the operator headcount reached 612. Voluntary turnover
among operators with less than one year of service fell from 34 percent
to 19 percent.

7. FLEET AND FACILITIES

RRTA received 18 battery-electric buses during the year, bringing the
zero-emission fleet to 42 vehicles, 25 percent of the active fleet. The
North Division garage completed the installation of 30 depot chargers
and a 1.2-megawatt solar canopy. Electric buses averaged 1.9 kilowatt-
hours per mile in FY2026; energy cost per mile was 61 percent lower than
for comparable diesel buses, although maintenance costs for the first
generation of batteries were higher than expected.

Construction of the Eastgate Transit Center reached 70 percent
completion, with opening planned for the spring of 2027. Forty-six bus
stops received new shelters, benches and lighting, prioritized by
ridership and by equity criteria.

8. FINANCIAL SUMMARY

Operating expenses totaled $162.4 million, 2.8 percent under the
adopted budget of $167.1 million. Sources of operating revenue were:

Table 2. Operating revenue, FY2026 (millions)
Local sales tax (half-cent transit tax)    $ 98.7
Fares and passes                           $ 14.9
State operating assistance                 $ 21.6
Federal formula funds (preventive maint.)  $ 19.3
Advertising and other                      $  3.4
Total                                      $157.9

The $4.5 million difference between expenses and revenue was covered by
the operating reserve, which ended the year at $38.2 million, equal to
2.8 months of operating expenses and above the board policy minimum of
two months. The farebox recovery ratio was 9.2 percent.

Capital spending reached $71.8 million, mostly for the Blue Line,
electric buses and the Eastgate Transit Center, funded 62 percent by
federal grants.

9. LOOKING AHEAD TO FY2027

The FY2027 budget, adopted on June 18, 2026, totals $171.5 million for
operations. The main priorities are:

- Service: the fall service change effective October 4, 2026 extends
  15-minute frequency to Routes 8 and 19 and adds late-night trips on the
  Red Line until 1 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.
- Reliability: bus lanes on Fourth Street and Grant Boulevard, to be
  installed by the City of Riverbend in spring 2027.
- Finances: the half-cent transit tax expires on December 31, 2028.
  The Board will decide by June 2027 whether to ask voters to renew it.
  Without renewal, RRTA would lose 62 percent of its operating revenue.
- Fleet: an order for 24 more battery-electric buses, with deliveries
  through 2028.

The full audited financial statements are available in the Annual
Comprehensive Financial Report, published separately.
